1:
With Job's long reply ended, Bildad the Shuhite rises a second time, and the witnesses feel at once how the temper of the debate has hardened. The reformed John Gill marks the change of manner: coming after Eliphaz, Bildad now attacks Job more roughly and severely than before, giving him no advice or counsel, no instruction, no hint that better times might come, but only heaping up charges and painting the misery of a wicked man as near to Job's own case as he can, that he may confirm his old thesis — the wicked are punished, therefore a man so greatly afflicted must be wicked. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the speech as passionate invective: irritated past bearing that Job should treat their counsel with contempt, Bildad can no longer keep his passions within the bounds of decency, and passes to downright abuse, trying to terrify Job into compliance by drawing a yet more dreadful picture of the wicked man's end than any before, and throwing in every circumstance of Job's calamities so that the resemblance cannot be missed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears Bildad shoot his arrows — bitter words — against poor Job, little thinking that, wise and good man though he was, in this he served Satan's design of adding to Job's affliction. Henry gathers the charges the speech opens with: idle, endless talk; a regardlessness of what was said to him; a haughty disdain that counts his friends as beasts; an outrageous passion that tears his own soul; and a proud expectation to give law to Providence itself. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes only that Bildad begins very much as Job himself had done at the head of an earlier speech in chapter 16.

Behind them all stands the latin-fathers voice of Gregory the Great, who reads the whole scene as the adversary's last device. Having failed to bring Job down by the loss of his substance and his children, and failed again through the goading of his wife, the enemy of the human race betook himself to other appliances of tempting: he brought in the friends as if to administer consolation, yet stirred their feelings to bitterness of upbraiding, that the man whom scourges had not subdued might at least be overcome by bitter words in the midst of those scourges. The witnesses do not divide; together they set Bildad's harsher second speech in its true light — a wise man's tongue bent, unawares, to the tempter's purpose.
2:
Bildad opens with a complaint of endless talk, and the witnesses puzzle both over whom he addresses and over the odd Hebrew word beneath the phrase. The reformed John Gill notes that "make an end of words" is put in the plural, so that some take more persons than one to be addressed — Eliphaz and Job together, or all the friends, whom Bildad chides for not stopping Job's mouth at once and suffering the dispute to be drawn out; why wait, he seems to ask, till such a hardened and conceited man has done, when it is all labour in vain, mere beating the air, and high time the debate were ended. The wesleyan-arminian voices read the plural differently. Adam Clarke thinks it means all present — "it is vain to talk with this man, and follow him through all his quibbles" — while John Wesley takes it as a common idiom of the Eastern tongue, speaking of one person, Job, in the plural because he was a man of eminence, and glosses the following "mark" as a call to consider the matter better.

The deeper crux is the word rendered "make an end." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "how long will ye hunt for words?" — Bildad, who is himself at pains throughout to be brief, reproaching the others with a chase after speeches that never ends; yet they concede that if the word be derived from the root for "end," it yields no clear sense unless it be "how long will ye make close upon close, beginning ever anew?" Clarke labours the philology at length: the form is a Chaldee one, and the word may come either from a root meaning "end" or "limit," or from a root meaning "thorn," so that Mr. Good would render "how long will ye plant thorns" — lacerating invectives — "among words"; while Schultens, taking it as the Arabic for hunting or laying snares, would read "how long will you put captious snares in words?"

The witnesses thus circle a single line by three roads — an end of words, a hunt for words, or thorns and snares set among them — and though they do not settle the Hebrew, they agree on its drift: Bildad is out of patience, and means to have done with hearing Job and to bury him under a speech of his own. Gill catches the irony that the man impatient of others' words is himself about to pour out a long one.
3:
The charge that stings Bildad most is that Job has, he thinks, reckoned his friends no better than brutes. The reformed John Gill traces the grievance to Job's earlier words — his sending them to the beasts of the field for instruction in chapter 12, and his complaint of their want of wisdom in chapter 17 — from which Bildad infers that Job has counted them as beasts and set them below himself. Gill turns the complaint back with a quiet irony: man by the fall is indeed become like the beasts, and those most sensible of themselves are readiest to own that they are brutish and as a beast before God, especially in the deep matters of providence that were the very thing in dispute; but self-sufficient men will not have their understandings called in question, and say with the Pharisees, "are we blind also?" in John 9.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the sense plain: Adam Clarke paraphrases, "thou treatest us as if we had neither reason nor understanding," and John Wesley glosses "beasts" as ignorant and stupid men, pointing back to Job's words in chapter 17. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott traces the reference to Job's contempt in chapter 13 and chapter 16, and marks the shape of the whole speech: here there is a marked increase in Bildad's harshness and violence, yet the chapter has a certain likeness to his first speech in chapter 8, for as there, so here, he works out a single extended simile — and, Ellicott notes, at v.16 the two similes touch, the tree with its dried roots and severed branch reappearing.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Whether Job had literally likened them to beasts or only slighted their wisdom, Bildad has taken it as the deepest of affronts, and, as Gill observes, a proud spirit is apt to think itself despised more than it really is, and a hot spirit is glad of a pretence to be hard on the man it means to condemn. Gill presses the point home: the wisest of men are the readiest to confess how little they know of the deep ways of God's providence, so that Bildad's very resentment of the charge betrays the self-sufficiency it denies, and the friends who will not be thought ignorant are, in this at least, the more ignorant for it. The plural "we," Ellicott adds, need not surprise us, for Job is regarded as the representative of a class, or the plural is used, as we still use it, in addressing a single person. The offence, real or fancied, is the spark that kindles the long invective to follow.
4:
"He teareth himself in his anger" — and the witnesses hear in the taunt a double stroke, first at Job's supposed madness and then at his supposed pride. The reformed John Gill notes that the Hebrew is "his soul," and that Bildad, taking up Job's own earlier words about tearing, throws them back: it is neither God nor man that tears you, it is you yourself; Job is made out a madman, rending his flesh and even his soul, his own passion doing him more hurt than all his losses — a charge of impatience, Gill adds, that ill suits the true character of Job. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, sharpens it: "thou art a madman; thy fury so sways thee that thou eatest thy own flesh."

Then comes the retort upon Job's complaint, and here the witnesses find a genuine misuse of Scripture. "Shall the earth be forsaken for thee?" Clarke reads as a rebuke of monstrous pride: afflictions are the common lot of men; must God work a miracle in providence to exempt thee alone? John Wesley expands the two questions — shall God give over the government of the earth for thy sake, to still thy clamours? shall the counsels of God, more immoveable than rocks, and the whole course of his providence, be altered to comply with thy humours? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott exposes the sleight of hand. As Eliphaz had done in chapter 15, Bildad treats Job as a maniac whose teaching would banish God from the earth and remove the strength and hope of man; and the closing clause, about the rock removed out of its place, is lifted straight from Job's own mouth in chapter 14, where Job had used it very differently. It looks, Ellicott says, like a wilful perversion of Job's words, or at the least a turning of them to Bildad's own purposes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lesson without excusing the speaker. When we quarrel with the events of Providence we forget that whatever befalls us is according to the eternal counsel of God, according to his written word — for it is written that in the world we shall have tribulation — and according to the settled track of his providence, nothing but what is common to men; and to expect that God's counsels should change and his word fail to please us is as absurd as to think the earth should be forsaken and the rock removed for our sake. The rebuke, Henry allows, has truth in it, though Bildad aims it unjustly; the earth is not forsaken for any man, and the sooner Job's passion owns it the better. The witnesses converge: the taunt is cruel and its proof-text abused, yet the providence it appeals to stands.
5:
Here Bildad turns from the man to his doom, and launches the long description of the wicked man's ruin that fills the rest of the chapter. The reformed John Gill reads the opening "yea" as "nevertheless" — whatever Job's rage and pride, this shall certainly be his case — and takes the light that is put out not as the light of the eye or of outward estate but as the moral light of nature, that inward lamp by which every man discerns things civil and religious, which, when it is abused, God may justly take away, giving the sinner up to judicial blindness and a reprobate mind; he notes that Cocceius understood it rather of the light of doctrine and knowledge. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, would even read the clause as a wish or imprecation — "let the light of the wicked be extinguished" — the abused understanding of a bad man justly taken from him, and marks that from this verse to the chapter's end the speech is one continual invective.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the imagery and a disputed word. "Yea," they agree, is here equivalent to "nevertheless"; the light of the evil-doer goes out, and the comfortable brightness his fire threw through the tent comes to an end, so that the lamp hanging above him is quenched — the very figure, they observe, that the Arab still uses when he says of a sudden misfortune, "fate has put out my lamp." The word rendered "spark," they note, occurs only here in Hebrew, and is read variously: Raschi and others take it for a spark or "tincelle," while the Septuagint, Theodotion, the Syriac and Jerome make it a flame, and the Targum the mere brightness of light.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the figure toward its moral. He grants that the wicked may have some light for a while — some pleasure, some hope, some wealth and honour — but it is a spark only, and a candle, easily blown out; not the light of the Lord, which is sunlight, but the light of his own fire and of sparks of his own kindling, as in Isaiah 50. And it will surely be put out: even in the tabernacle of the body the light shall be darkness, no solid comfort, no supporting hope; and when death puts him out of that tabernacle his candle is put out with him, for when a wicked man dies his expectation perishes, as Proverbs 11 has it, and he lies down in sorrow. Henry is careful, though, to enter the caveat that runs through all his comment on the chapter: there is much certain truth here — that a sinful condition is a sad one, and sin will be a man's ruin unless he repent — but it was neither safe nor just of Bildad to apply it to Job, for not all who are brought low are therefore wicked. The witnesses converge on the certainty of the sentence while dividing, gently, over its object.
6:
The image narrows from light in general to the light of a man's own tent, and the witnesses read the darkening of the tabernacle as the eclipse of house and household. The reformed John Gill runs through the senses once more: not the light of the eye in the tabernacle of the body, but rather the light of nature and reason — for if the light that is in a man become darkness, how great is that darkness — though best of all, he thinks, the light of prosperity in his house and family, now quite obscured. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it wholly of outward ruin: his property destroyed, his house pillaged, himself and his family brought to an untimely end; and the candle put out with him he takes to mean that the man shall have no posterity, his lamp and his line extinguished together.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the figure of the tent-lamp they began at the previous verse: the light in his tent is changed, as the perfect tense implies, in one word into darkness, and the lamp that hangs from the covering above him — the lamp of chapter 29, they note — goes out; the fourfold repetition of the image of a quenched light drives home how total the reversal is. And they carry the picture forward into the next figure, that of the wicked man's steps, once free and vigorous, now straitened and hemmed in, comparing the straitened going of Proverbs 4, where the upright man's steps are, by contrast, not straitened.

The witnesses do not divide. Whether the darkened light be reason, or comfort, or the prosperity of a home, they agree that Bildad means the man's whole world to go black at once — the fire on his hearth cold, the lamp over his bed spent, and no child left to relight it. Gill's caution about the several senses only enriches the picture: the sinner loses inward peace and outward plenty and future hope in a single stroke, and the candle that is "put out with him" seals the ruin by carrying it past his own death into the extinction of his name. It is, on every reading, a portrait of darkness closing over a tent that had once been bright, and it prepares the ground for the snares and terrors that Bildad will now spring one after another upon his victim.
7:
With the light gone dark, Bildad turns to the wicked man's gait, and the witnesses read the straitening of his strong steps as the narrowing of a life once wide and free. The reformed John Gill draws the contrast from health and sickness: as a man in vigour takes large, strong strides and travels in the greatness of his strength, so in prosperity he walks at liberty, goes in and out at pleasure, and none controls him; but in adversity his strength is weakened in the way, his path hedged up with thorns, and, turn which way he will, he can find no room to escape. John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, reads "the steps of his strength" by a Hebraism as his strong steps — his attempts and enterprises, those contrived with the greatest strength of understanding and pushed with the greatest resolution — now hindered and entangled, so that he cannot proceed or accomplish what he designs.

Adam Clarke keeps the same sense but adds a sharper edge: even in his greatest prosperity the wicked man shall be in straits, and "his own counsel" shall cast him down, for he is the dupe and victim of his own airy, ambitious, and impious schemes. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "the steps of his strength" as his giant strides, and presses the same irony: he shall be the victim of his own devices, which, at the very moment they seem to hold out the hope of prosperity, lead him to destruction.

Here Clarke opens a reading that will govern the next verses. From this point to v.13, he says, the language is drawn throughout from the arts of the hunt: a company of men spread through a forest and drive the game before them, straitening the ground from a broad base to a narrow point, the hunters lining each side and the dogs coming up behind — and this, he suggests, is the very picture behind "the steps of his strength shall be straitened," the quarry's room growing less at every stride. The witnesses do not divide. Whether the straitening be read of a sick man's failing steps, of an ambitious man tripped by his own plots, or of a hunted beast herded into an ever-narrowing space, all agree that the wicked man's own strength and his own counsel are made the instruments of his fall, so that he needs no enemy but himself.
8:
Now the hunting-imagery breaks fully open, and the witnesses observe how Bildad heaps up, verse upon verse, every word he can find for a trap. The reformed John Gill fastens on the tragic clause "by his own feet": the wicked man goes into the net of himself, incautious and imprudent, so that the counsels he laid to hurt others issue in his own ruin — the pit he digs he falls into, the net he spread for another takes his own foot, and the very sins he commits are snares that entice and hold him, for, as the proverb says, in the transgression of an evil man there is a snare. Gill notes an alternative rendering, that the man goes with a net already at his feet, hampered at every step. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads it of a beast that has blundered into the toils: his own conduct brings him to ruin, and, like a wild thing taken in a net, the more he flounces to free himself the more he is entangled; he is forever walking upon the meshes that must soon close over him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the verse against Job's own complaint. Job had pictured himself as one hunted by the Almighty in chapter 10; Bildad now describes the evil man snared in a net, but a net for which he has no one to thank but himself — it is his own pit he falls into — and the insinuation, Ellicott says, is plain: Job too is responsible for his calamities, which are the just punishment of his sin. Ellicott adds the observation that unlocks the whole passage: in this verse and those that follow the speaker deliberately heaps together every term the language affords for the art of snaring, net after gin after trap, as if to hem the wicked man in with words as tightly as the hunter hems in his prey.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the force of the verse lies in that one phrase, "by his own feet" — the ruin is self-inflicted, the sinner walking with open eyes onto the very ground that will betray him. Whether the figure be a man tangled in his own plots or a beast blundering into the net, the moral is the same, and it is the moral Bildad presses cruelly upon Job: that the trap which holds a man fast was set and sprung by his own feet, and that his misery is therefore the measure of his guilt.
9:
The gin closes on the heel, and a robber falls upon the fugitive, and the witnesses divide over who that robber is. The reformed John Gill keeps to the figure of the trap: the gin holds him fast so that he cannot get away, and he reminds the reader that God himself has nets and snares and gins in plenty for wicked men — is even said to rain them down, and is himself a snare to them — so that to fall into his hands is a fearful thing from which there is no escape. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in "the robber" a person, and names him: it is Satan who shall prevail against the sinner, for as he was a murderer, so he was a robber, from the beginning; the tempter lays his snares in every path, and if he makes men sinful like himself he will make them miserable like himself, hunting, Henry says, for the precious life.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the relentless step-by-step march of the description toward total destruction, every clause bearing the marks of a curse being fulfilled, and render the pair of lines with the gin seizing the heel and the noose drawing tight. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, notes that Houbigant would read v.10 before this one — the snare laid in the ground, then the gin taking the heel — and unfolds the whole hunt he sees behind verses seven to thirteen: after the game is driven into the narrowing ground, nets and gins and pitfalls are set so that many are taken before the lines close; the howling of dogs and the shouts of men drive the beast on beyond its strength; and at last, spent and entangled, it is pierced or hamstrung, so that "the robber shall prevail against him" pictures the huntsman falling on his exhausted quarry.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense, only over the figure's reach. Gill and Clarke see a hunted beast overpowered at the net; Henry lifts the same "robber" into the person of the tempter who has stalked the sinner all along and now claims his prey; Keil and Delitzsch hold the two together, a doom both natural and moral, the outward capture the visible form of an inward curse. What none of them doubts is that the heel once caught cannot be drawn back: the sinner may as soon overpower the divine omnipotence as flee the divine omniscience, and the gin that has taken him holds by an appointment he cannot break.
10:
The single verse names two more instruments — a snare hidden in the earth, a trap set in the path — and the witnesses dwell on the cunning of concealment. The reformed John Gill explains why the snare is "laid," or rather hidden, in the ground: in vain, says the wise man, is the net spread in the sight of any bird, for a creature that sees the trap will shun it; and so the fowler buries his snare out of sight where his quarry is likely to tread, and keeps the very cord that springs it hidden in his hand, that nothing may warn the prey. He points, for the proverb, to the opening of Proverbs 1, where the net is spread in vain before the watching bird.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, carrying on their rendering of the strophe, set the two clauses in parallel — his snare lies hidden in the earth, his nets upon the path — so that whether the wicked man stands still or walks on, a device is ready for him; there is no safe ground and no safe road. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, folds the verse into the hunt he has been describing: this is the stage at which the pitfalls and gins are set within the narrowing ground, "the trap laid for him in the way, the snare in the ground," so that many are taken before ever they reach the point where the lines of beaters close.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the perfection of the trap's cruelty — that it is unseen. The sinner walks a path that looks open and treads a ground that looks firm, and the very hiddenness of the snare is what makes it sure; he can take no precaution against a danger he cannot detect. Bildad means, of course, that Job's calamities fell so because a hidden justice had long prepared them; but the witnesses, taking the imagery on its own terms, let it say something truer than Bildad intends — that the ways of sin are mined with concealed ruin, and that the man who walks them confidently is the likeliest of all to be caught. The snare in the ground and the trap in the way wait, silent, for a foot that suspects nothing. And Gill lets the figure widen into a warning of God's own hidden snares, out of which, once sprung, there is no getting free; the fowler's buried cord becomes, on his reading, an emblem of a justice that prepares in secret what it means at last openly to execute.
11:
"Terrors shall make him afraid on every side" — Bildad turns from the snare to the dread that hounds the man into it, and the witnesses gather round the haunting of a guilty mind. The reformed John Gill makes the wicked man a very "Magor-missabib," a terror round about like Pashur in Jeremiah 20, and multiplies the terrors that beset him: the terrors of earthly judges, before whom evildoers tremble; the terrors of a guilty conscience, that make an hell on earth; the terrors of the broken law with its menaces of death; the terrors of God's judgments hanging over the world; and, underlying all, the dread of divine wrath here and hereafter, and of death itself. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the closing verb, comparing the fear that comes suddenly in chapter 15: one is tempted, he says, to read that the terrors "startle him to his feet," as the English suggests, but the truer meaning is probably that they "chase him at his heels," dogging him step for step.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening here the great description that carries to the chapter's end, dwells on the restlessness of a haunted conscience. The terrors of his own guilt shall follow the sinner wherever he goes and stare him in the face whichever way he looks; it will make him tremble to see himself fought against by the whole creation — heaven frowning on him, hell gaping for him, and earth sick of him. The man who carries his own accuser and his own tormentor always in his bosom cannot but be afraid on every side; and this it is that drives him to his feet, like the malefactor who flees when none pursues, as in Proverbs 28. Yet his feet, Henry adds with grim point, will do him no service, for they are already fast in the snare of the verse before: the sinner may flee the pursuer, but he cannot flee the divine omniscience that is the pursuer.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the whip which drives the wicked man forward is inward — not first the sword of an enemy but the terror of his own soul — so that the way of sin is itself a way of fear. Gill's crowd of terrors and Henry's haunted conscience meet in one figure: a man surrounded, startled at every sound, running he knows not where, because the accuser he flees from he carries within. Bildad wields the picture as a weapon against Job; the witnesses receive it as a true account of what unrepented guilt does to the heart that harbours it.
12:
The wicked man's strength is now said to be "hungerbitten," and the witnesses weigh both what that strength is and how the ruin waits beside it. The reformed John Gill first reads the word as famine itself — his strength shall be famine-struck, weakened as the natural force of the strongest man is soon brought down when the staff of bread is taken from him — but records that many Jewish writers understand "his strength" of his children, who are, as Jacob said of Reuben in Genesis 49, a man's might and the beginning of his strength; the Targum names his firstborn son, Jarchi his son, Ben Gersom his seed. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, notes the same option — some, comparing that verse of Genesis, take "his strength" for the firstborn son — but judges it needless to depart from the plain sense of bodily strength; and he offers a second reading of the next clause, that "destruction ready at his side" may rather mean ready "for his halting," lying in wait for his tripping in order to overthrow him.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, keeps the picture of the exhausted quarry: spent with hunger and the long chase, the beast is easily taken, so that "his strength is hunger-bitten, and destruction is ready at his side"; and he cites the Chaldee paraphrase, which turns the verse cruelly upon a man's household — "let his firstborn son be famished, and affliction be prepared for his wife." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the failing strength inwardly: that which the sinner relied on as his strength — his wealth, his power, his pomp, his friends, the hardiness of his own spirit — shall fail him in the hour of need and be hunger-bitten, doing him no more service than a famished man would do in work or war, while destruction stands ready at his side to seize him the moment justice gives the word, so that he is brought into desolation in a moment, as in Psalm 73.

So the witnesses part gently over the word "strength" — whether it names the man's own vigour and resources, worn out and useless when the blow falls, or his children, the strength of his house, cut off by famine before him — and they let both senses stand, for Bildad's picture is large enough to hold them. On either reading the point is the same: whatever the wicked man leaned on is eaten away from within just as the outward stroke draws near, so that ruin finds him already too weak to resist it, and "ready at his side" means only that it need not even seek him out.
13:
The verse names a strange and dreadful figure — "the firstborn of death" — and the witnesses divide both over what it devours and over what it is. On the first clause, the reformed John Gill offers "the bars of his skin" or "the branches of his skin," the veins that run beneath and show through it, and reads the devouring as famine wasting a man to a skeleton, blackening his skin like an oven; yet he records that the Targum, Jarchi, and Aben Ezra take those "bars" or "branches" for the man's children, the strength that proceeds from him as branches from a tree. The grammatical-historical voices prefer the body. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the members here called "bars" are the parts into which the body branches out, and that the skin is the surface of the naked body, which "the firstborn of death" devours gradually but surely and entirely; Charles Ellicott would render the whole, "it shall devour the members of his body, even the firstborn of death shall devour his members."

On the haunting phrase itself the readings multiply. Keil and Delitzsch, comparing "the firstborn of the poor" in Isaiah 14 — meaning the poor in the highest degree — take "the firstborn of death" for the most deadly of diseases, disease conceived as death's eldest and strongest child. Ellicott agrees that it is probably some wasting disease such as Job's own, the phrase used as a grim euphemism. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, keeping his hunt, reads it rather as a sudden and overwhelming stroke that deprives the trapped animal of life, and cites the Chaldee, "the angel of death shall consume his children." John Wesley calls it simply a terrible kind of death, the firstborn being the chief among brethren, so that the title is given to whatever is eminent in its kind — here, death at its most fearful.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sense into the deathbed scene: the sinner is arrested by the firstborn of death, some disease or stroke that carries in it a more than common resemblance of death itself — "so great a death," as Paul calls it in 2 Corinthians 1 — a messenger of uncommon strength and terror, which devours the strength of his skin and brings rottenness into his bones. So the witnesses circle a phrase none of them will flatten: is "the firstborn of death" a wasting sickness, death's deadliest child, as Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott hold; a sudden mortal blow, as Clarke reads it; or simply death in its most terrible form, as Wesley and Henry take it? They do not settle it, and the very obscurity serves Bildad's design, for the undefined dread is the more frightening; but they agree that whatever it is, it eats the man up by degrees, skin and members and strength, until nothing of him is left to devour.
14:
With the body wasted, Bildad tears away the man's last security and marches him to a dreadful king. The reformed John Gill turns over what "his confidence" may be — his wealth and children, in which he trusted for future happiness; or his sound constitution, on which he counted for long life; or his very hope of eternal happiness — and offers also the rendering that reverses the clause: "he shall be rooted out of his tabernacle, which was his confidence," the soul plucked by death out of the body it had dwelt in and hoped long to keep. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, prefers just that turn: "he shall be rooted out of his tent, which he trusted was his own." John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, keeps the plainer sense — all the matter of his confidence, his riches and his children, torn from him.

The knot of the verse is "the king of terrors," and here the witnesses genuinely differ. Wesley takes it flatly for death, which even Aristotle called the most terrible of all terribles, and which does its work either by exposing the man to enemies who kill him or by breaking his heart with the sense of his losses. Ellicott exalts the phrase as perhaps the most remarkable personification of unseen forces to be found in the whole Bible. But Adam Clarke will not have it so easily. The words "king of terrors," he argues, have been generally taken for death, yet the Hebrew does not warrant the beautiful phrase: one of De Rossi's manuscripts reads "as a king," and the versions point rather to "it shall tread upon him as a king," or "as a destroyer"; Mr. Good renders "dissolution shall invade him as a monarch," and Coverdale, "very fearfulness shall bring him to the king." Clarke is glad to record the caution of the Bishop of Killala, who was sorry to part with so fine an expression but owned there was no authority for it in the text — even while granting that death was in fact styled by like titles among the Greeks and Latins, Virgil's king of hell and Sophocles' Pluto, king of shades.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, untroubled by the philology, preaches the phrase. The sinner, surrounded all his life by terrors, is at length brought as a captive to the conqueror; death is the king of all those terrors, terrible to nature — our Saviour himself prayed, "Father, save me from this hour," in John 12 — but to the wicked in a special manner the king of terrors, both as it ends the life in which they placed their happiness and as it opens the life where they find their misery; whereas to the saints, Henry rejoices, this king of terrors is by Christ so far disarmed that he becomes a friend and servant. So the witnesses hold two things at once: a vivid, awful figure of death enthroned, which Ellicott and Henry embrace and Wesley reads plainly, and a textual doubt, pressed by Clarke, whether Bildad said quite so much — a doubt that leaves the terror standing even if the crown is uncertain.
15:
An unnamed dweller takes possession of the empty tent, and brimstone falls on the roof, and the witnesses first ask who or what it is that moves in. The reformed John Gill owns that the text does not say — "it shall dwell in his tabernacle," but what "it" is is left blank, and the conjectures are many. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, personifies Desolation: it shall be the inhabitant now that the former owner is destroyed, and he adorns the thought with a Persian couplet in which the spider is the only chamberlain left in Caesar's palace and the owl the only sentinel on a conqueror's watchtower. John Wesley makes the dweller the Destruction named two verses back, come to fix its abode with him. But Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, reads a different Hebrew: "there shall dwell in his tent they that are none of his" — strangers taking over a home that is no longer his, or, he hints, that was never rightly his, having been violently seized from someone else.

That last thought turns on the clause "because it is none of his," and here Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry agree: the habitation is doomed because it was unjustly got, kept by deceit or violence from its rightful owner, so that the man may look neither for the comfort nor the continuance of it. Henry lets even the dwelling share the owner's curse, death itself taking possession of the tent from which its master has been expelled. On the brimstone the witnesses are nearly one, with a single dissent. Wesley, Henry, and Ellicott all hear an allusion to Sodom and the cities of the plain in Genesis 19 — the habitation utterly destroyed, as by fire and brimstone, and made an everlasting monument of the divine displeasure. Clarke offers the same first, then adds a second possibility: brimstone was anciently scattered to purify and hallow a house, as Pliny and Ovid attest, and as the rites Servius describes made purgation by fire and sulphur, by water, and by wind; yet Clarke himself judges it most likely that Bildad, in his unkind way, is glancing at the actual destruction of Job's property and family by fire and storm — the fire of God that fell on the sheep, and the great wind that smote the house where his children feasted, in chapter 1.

The witnesses do not finally divide, for the several readings deepen rather than contradict one another. Whether the new tenant be personified Desolation, or a swarm of strangers, and whether the brimstone recall Sodom or the purging of a defiled house, the verse leaves the same desolate scene: a home emptied of its owner, taken over by what is not his, and marked with the smell of sulphur as a place under judgment. And in Clarke's reading the cruelty is sharpest, for Bildad points the whole picture at the still-smoking ruin of Job's own house.
16:
Bildad returns to the tree he had planted in his first speech, and the witnesses watch it wither from root to branch. The reformed John Gill reads the drying of the roots as the extinction of the man's family, the stock from which he sprang now cut off with him, or else the exhausting of his substance: having seemed to take root in the earth, spreading and settled, he is now, like Ephraim in the prophet, smitten and his root dried up, every resource of his wealth run dry. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, makes the ruin total — the man destroyed in himself, his posterity, and his property alike, as a tree whose every branch is lopped and whose every root is cut away.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the deliberate echo. This is a tacit allusion, he says, to what Bildad had said before of the godless man's plant in chapter 8, and, more cruelly, to the destruction of Job's own offspring, which had already come to pass; the figure of the drying root and the severed branch is not idle poetry but a pointed reminder of children already dead. It is the very tree, moreover, that Bildad had raised at the outset of his speech, so that, as Ellicott had observed at the head of the chapter, the two similes of the discourse here touch and close upon one another, the root beneath and the branch above blasted in a single stroke.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lesson wide and then turns it to hope. The wicked man's roots dried up beneath and his branch cut off above is the fate of the great houses that took root only in the earth — the houses of Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab, of which none was left alive; those who consult the true honour and welfare of their family will be afraid of withering it by sin. But Henry sets against the blasted tree the promise of a better rooting: those who are rooted not in the earth but in Christ shall find that even their leaf does not wither, much less their branch cut off — and so the very image Bildad uses to threaten becomes, rightly taken, an invitation. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Bildad means the sinner's utter extirpation, stock and shoot, self and seed, and that he aims the threat at a man freshly bereaved of his children; and they agree, too, that the threat holds only of a life rooted in the perishing earth, not of one hidden, as Job's finally was, in the God who kills and makes alive.
17:
From the man's body and household Bildad passes to his memory, and the witnesses read the blotting-out of a name as the last and deepest of his losses. The reformed John Gill observes that the wicked are forgotten not only in heaven, remembered by God only for judgment, but on earth, in the very places where they lived; even the houses and palaces and cities they built to perpetuate their memory perish and carry their memorial down with them. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, keeps it terse: the man shall leave none to survive him and continue his name, and shall never be a man of reputation, so that after his death none will so much as talk of his fame. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, adds a telling touch from the world of the book: to perish from remembrance is, above all others, the doom dreaded by the roamers of the desert, for whom a surviving name is the one immortality — a dread he sets beside the promise of a lasting name in Jeremiah 35.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, take up here the run of clauses that carries to the chapter's end, rendering the wicked man's remembrance perished from the earth and no name left him in the street, then driven from light into darkness and chased out of the world. They pause on the phrase "his day," by which, as in Hebrew and Arabic alike, is meant the day of a man's doom, the day appointed for his fall.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its sharpest antithesis. The wicked man's remembrance perishes from the earth, and if it perish thence it perishes wholly, for it was never written in heaven, as the names of the saints are in Luke 10; all his honour is laid in the dust or stained with lasting infamy, so that he has no name in the street and departs without being desired. Henry sets over the whole the proverb that the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot, from Proverbs 10. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Bildad reaches here for what an ancient man feared most — not merely to die, but to be forgotten, his very name struck from the street where he once walked in honour — and that he means Job, whose greatness was already fallen, to feel the threat of oblivion closing over a name that had once been great in the gate.
18:
The sentence of banishment is pronounced — driven from light, chased out of the world — and the witnesses hear in the violent verbs a death that is no quiet sleep. The reformed John Gill traces the light and the darkness through their senses: from the light of outward prosperity into the darkness of adversity, or rather from the light of the living into the darkness of death and the grave, the land of darkness and the shadow of death, and beyond that into the utter darkness that is set over against the inheritance of the saints in light. He lingers on the plural of the Hebrew, "they shall drive him," and finds in it more than one hand at the work — God driving him away in the storm of his wrath, or the angels, good or bad, hurrying him by divine commission into endless night. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads a violent death: the man is taken off, driven away in his iniquity, and the very word betrays his reluctance, for the wicked is dragged from a life he is loath to leave. John Wesley keeps it simple — from a prosperous life to disgrace and misery, and to the grave, the land of darkness.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, set the clause in the march of doom they have been rendering, the man chased out of the world as one hunted from the society of the living. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the pathos of the chasing. The sinner is hurried away sorely against his will, chased as Adam was out of paradise, for this world is his paradise and he is loath to depart; but all the world is weary of him and glad to be rid of him, and so he is thrust from the light of this life and its prosperous condition into darkness — the darkness of the grave, and, Henry does not shrink to say, the outer darkness where there is never a gleam of light again, as in Psalm 49.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Bildad paints not a natural close but an expulsion — a man driven, chased, dragged from the warm light of the living into a cold and final dark, unwilling every step. Gill's several hands, Clarke's violent stroke, Henry's Adam thrust from Eden, all render the same motion: the wicked man does not so much leave the world as get turned out of it, and the light he loved shuts behind him. It is among the harshest things Bildad has yet said, and, as Henry quietly reminds us, it is true only of a life that had no light but this world's to lose.
19:
Bildad drives home the extinction of the man's line — neither son nor grandson, none left where he lived — and the witnesses feel how nearly the stroke falls on Job. The reformed John Gill reads "nephew" in its old sense of a son's son, following the Targum, Jarchi, and Bar Tzemach: the wicked man shall be childless, with no heir or successor to inherit his estate and perpetuate his name among his people; and then Gill catches Bildad in his error, for though he plainly aims at Job, who had lost all his children, he was mistaken in the outcome — Job had afterward as many children as he had before. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, renders the doubled phrase precisely — neither his own son's son among his people, nor any remaining where he sojourned — the man cut off both in his posterity and in the very place of his sojourning. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, gives Coverdale's old version, which adds the onlookers' dismay: "he shall neither have children nor kinsfolk among his people, nor any posterity in his country; young and old shall be astonished at his death."

Keil and Delitzsch, carrying their rendering forward, keep the same double negation — no son nor grandchild among his people, none remaining in his dwellings — the household swept clean of every survivor. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the threat honestly against Job's case. Sin entails a curse upon posterity, he grants, and the iniquity of the fathers is often visited on the children; here, too, Bildad plainly reflects on the death of Job's children and servants as a further proof of his wickedness. But Henry will not let the inference stand: all that are written childless are not thereby written graceless, for there is a name better than that of sons and daughters, as the prophet promises in Isaiah 56.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only over its justice. They agree that Bildad means the sinner's family to be blotted out root and branch, no son to bear his name and no distant kinsman to keep his memory in the place he lived; and they agree, with Gill and Henry, that the taunt was aimed straight at a freshly bereaved man — and that in Job's case it proved false, God restoring the very posterity Bildad had pronounced forfeit. The verse stands, on their reading, as a warning of what sin does to a house, and as a caution against reading every childless grave as a mark of guilt.
20:
The onlookers now enter the picture, struck dumb at the wicked man's fall, and the witnesses debate who exactly they are. Most take the terms as marks of time. The reformed John Gill reads "they that come after" as those younger than the wicked man who outlive him, or posterity in later ages who hear the report, all thunderstruck that one so flourishing should be brought at a stroke, with his household, into such ruin. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, divides them the same way: the young are astonished when they hear the tale, and "they that went before" — the aged contemporaries who saw the judgment fall — were seized with horror, panic-struck. John Wesley agrees, reading those "before" as the men of the time and place where the judgment was inflicted, amazed at the suddenness and dreadfulness of it. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical, glosses "his day" as his doom or destiny, and makes the man a standing warning and monument to all who come after.

But Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, propose a different axis altogether. The two words, they argue, are better taken not of those who come after and those who went before in time, but of place — those who dwell in the west and those who dwell in the east — so that the verse means the whole world, from the setting to the rising of the sun, is astonished at the wicked man's day, trembling seizing the one quarter as amazement holds the other. So the debate is drawn: is the horror spread across the generations, the young hearing what the old saw, or across the compass, west and east alike aghast? Both readings make the fall a public and universal spectacle; they differ only over whether its witnesses are separated by years or by miles.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry cares less for the axis than for the awe. So sudden is the change, he says, so dreadful the execution, and so threatening to all around, that those who see it are affrighted and those who come after and hear of it are astonished, their ears made to tingle and their hearts to tremble, till they cry, "Lord, how terrible art thou in thy judgments!" A place or person utterly ruined is made an astonishment, as Scripture often warns in Deuteronomy 28. The witnesses do not divide over that effect, only over the reach of the audience; and whether we set the astonished onlookers before and after the man or to west and east of him, the verse does the same work in Bildad's mouth — it makes the sinner's doom a byword and a horror, a thing at which the world stands aghast, and means Job to see himself as that spectacle.
21:
Bildad closes with a flourish of finality — "surely such are the dwellings of the wicked" — and the witnesses read the summing-up as both a claim to settled wisdom and a scarcely veiled thrust at Job. The reformed John Gill gathers the whole picture into the verdict: such, and no other, are the dwellings of the wicked as Bildad has drawn them, the light darkened, the confidence rooted out, the brimstone scattered, none remaining; and he notes that the Targum turns the line into the very cry of the astonished onlookers of the verse before, uttering their horror over the ruin. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the couplet plainly — surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this the place of him that knoweth not God — as the formal seal of the whole discourse.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, both hear the barb beneath the generality. This, Clarke says, is given out as the common lot of the wicked, and particularly of him who knows not God — that is, of Job, for it is evident Bildad alludes to him; and Clarke breaks off in pity, "Poor Job! hard was thy lot, severe were thy sufferings." Ellicott makes the point of grammar carry the accusation: Bildad designedly uses the singular, "the place of him that knoweth not God," and there can be little doubt he as designedly meant this terrible and cruel picture to represent Job himself. The whole chapter, on their reading, has been an arrow aimed at one man, and only in the last line is the bow fully drawn.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the closing verse for the sum of the chapter's theology, tracing the wicked world's course from its root to its end. The beginning of all this misery, he says, is ignorance of God — and a wilful ignorance, since enough may be known of him to leave men inexcusable; they know not God, and then they commit all iniquity, as Pharaoh knew not the Lord and so would not obey his voice. And the end of it is utter destruction: such, so miserable, are the dwellings of the wicked, for vengeance will be taken on them that know not God, as the apostle warns in 2 Thessalonians 1. Let us therefore, Henry closes, stand in awe and not sin. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Bildad's grand conclusion is true of the man who truly knows not God, and false and cruel as aimed at Job, who did know him; and so the chapter ends as it began, with a solemn truth bent to an unjust purpose — the dwellings of the wicked rightly described, and a righteous man wrongly lodged among them.
